implementation_notes: The double is created at runtime and configured before use: Mock(spec=Clock) restricts it to the real API by taking its specification from the object, return_value (set at construction or by attribute) fixes the answer, and side_effect carries a failure to raise, an iterable of successive values or a callable that computes the answer from the arguments; chained attributes are configured in one step with configure_mock. The stdlib module is the replacement for the pile of hand-written stubs, and the documentation contrasts its action-then-assertion style with the record-replay style of other mocking frameworks, which is exactly the configuration-mode distinction.
code_sketch:
from unittest.mock import Mock

clock = Mock(spec=Clock)
clock.now.side_effect = [epoch, TimeoutError('clock unavailable')]

session = Session(clock, timedelta(minutes=30))
with pytest.raises(TimeoutError):
    session.check()
clock.now.assert_called()
pitfalls: Without spec/autospec the mock accepts any attribute, so a typo in the attribute name configures a mock nobody calls and the test passes vacuously.
side_effect as an iterable is exhausted silently: extra calls raise StopIteration, which surfaces as an unrelated failure inside the SUT.
Mocks are per-instance state, but a mock stored on a shared fixture or a class attribute is reused between tests unless the fixture is function-scoped.

variants.name: Hand-written fake class configured by constructor arguments
variants.idiom_name: reusable fake class with constructor parameters for the canned answers
variants.implementation_notes: A plain class implements the collaborator role and takes its answers as constructor arguments or attributes, so the test states exactly what it configures while mypy and IDEs still see a real implementation; raising inside the method is how a failure double is built. Prefer it when the fake carries logic (in-memory store, recorded calls for later assertions) or when a spec-less mock would hide a typo, and keep the mock-based form for wide interfaces where hand-writing every member is noise. The same class is reusable across tests, which is the pattern's whole point.
pitfalls: Mutable attributes make the fake stateful across tests if it is created once per module rather than per test.
A hand-written fake drifts from the real collaborator silently; at least one test must run against the real implementation.
Fakes that collect calls grow without bound in long-running suites unless the collected data is cleared or the fake is re-created.
